articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Iran-Related Designations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on November 23, 2026. This action is part of ongoing efforts to target entities and individuals supporting the Iranian regime's destabilizing activities.

Further details regarding the specific individuals or entities designated, and the nature of their activities, are expected to be released by OFAC. These designations typically result in the blocking of all property and interests in property of the designated persons that are in the United States or in the possession or control of U.S. persons.

U.S. persons are generally prohibited from engaging in any transactions with designated individuals or entities. These measures aim to disrupt financial networks and procurement efforts that enable Iran's proliferation of weapons of mass destruction, support for terrorism, and human rights abuses.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Iran Designations and Cuba FAQs
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations related to Iran on November 20, 2026. Concurrently, OFAC issued new Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) concerning Cuba sanctions.

The Iran designations aim to further pressure the Iranian regime by targeting individuals and entities involved in various illicit activities. The issuance of Cuba FAQs provides updated guidance and clarification for individuals and entities engaging in Cuba-related transactions, reflecting the evolving policy landscape.
These actions underscore OFAC's commitment to enforcing sanctions programs against adversaries while also providing necessary clarity for compliance within complex regulatory environments.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Counter Narcotics and Cyber Actors, Amends Russia GL
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a series of designations on November 19, 2026, targeting individuals and entities involved in counter narcotics and cyber-related illicit activities. This action highlights the U.S. government's commitment to combating global illicit networks.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC issued an Illicit Drugs General License to facilitate certain humanitarian or other authorized transactions. Furthermore, an amended Russia-related General License and associated Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) were published, providing updated guidance for transactions involving Russia.

These measures aim to disrupt the financial infrastructure of criminal organizations and malicious cyber actors, while also adapting sanctions policies to address evolving geopolitical circumstances and humanitarian considerations.

articles.headline: OFAC Implements New Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new counter terrorism designations on November 18, 2026. These designations target individuals and entities identified as supporting terrorist organizations and activities globally.

The action is part of a broader strategy to disrupt the financial networks of terrorist groups and prevent them from accessing the international financial system. Designated parties face asset freezes and prohibitions on transactions with U.S. persons.
These measures underscore the U.S. government's ongoing efforts to safeguard national security and combat the financing of terrorism worldwide.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities for Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations on November 13, 2026, targeting individuals and entities involved in both counter narcotics and counter terrorism activities. This dual focus highlights the interconnected nature of various illicit finance threats.

These designations aim to disrupt the financial and logistical support networks that enable drug trafficking and terrorist operations. By targeting these illicit networks, OFAC seeks to protect the U.S. financial system from abuse.
The action reinforces the U.S. government's commitment to using its sanctions authorities to combat a wide range of national security threats.

articles.headline: OFAC Updates Iran Designation Information
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) published an update to its Iran designation information on November 9, 2026. This update likely involves modifications to existing listings or clarifications regarding previously designated individuals or entities.
Such updates are routine and ensure the accuracy and effectiveness of OFAC's sanctions lists. They may include changes to identifying information, aliases, or other details relevant to compliance.
Financial institutions and other regulated entities are advised to review these updates carefully to ensure their sanctions screening programs remain current and effective.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Iran-Related Designations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on November 6, 2026. These actions are part of the ongoing pressure campaign against the Iranian regime.

The designations target individuals and entities involved in activities that support Iran's destabilizing behavior, including its nuclear program, ballistic missile development, and support for regional proxy groups.
These measures aim to further isolate Iran from the international financial system and limit its ability to fund illicit activities.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Cyber and TCO Actors, Adds Cuba Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations on November 5, 2026, targeting cyber-related malicious actors and transnational criminal organizations (TCOs). This action underscores the U.S. government's focus on combating evolving threats in the digital and criminal spheres.

In addition to these designations, OFAC also implemented new Cuba designations and published a Cuba-related determination. These measures reflect a continued effort to address threats to U.S. national security and foreign policy interests.
The designations aim to disrupt the financial infrastructure of these illicit networks, while the Cuba-related actions further refine the U.S. sanctions policy towards the island nation.

articles.headline: OFAC Implements Iran Designations, Updates Listings, and Amends Venezuela GL

OFAC also published an Iran-related alert, providing guidance and warnings regarding potential sanctions evasion schemes. Concurrently, an amended Venezuela-related General License and a new Frequently Asked Question (FAQ) were issued, offering updated guidance for transactions involving Venezuela.

These comprehensive measures aim to enhance the effectiveness of sanctions against Iran while also providing necessary flexibility and clarity for humanitarian and other authorized activities in Venezuela.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an amended Iran-related General License on October 29, 2026. This amendment modifies existing authorizations for certain transactions involving Iran.

General Licenses are often issued to permit specific types of transactions that would otherwise be prohibited by sanctions, typically for humanitarian aid, personal remittances, or other activities deemed consistent with U.S. foreign policy objectives.
Entities and individuals engaging in Iran-related activities should review the amended General License to ensure ongoing compliance with OFAC regulations.

articles.headline: EU Council Approves New Strategic Vision for Outermost Regions
body: Ministers responsible for cohesion policies within the European Union approved conclusions on a new strategic vision for the EU's outermost regions on November 23, 2026. These regions include Guadeloupe, French Guiana, Martinique, Réunion, Mayotte, Saint-Martin, the Azores, Madeira, and the Canary Islands.

This approval follows a Commission communication presented on September 10, 2026, titled 'Strengthening the Union's global reach: a new strategic vision for the EU's outermost regions.' The conclusions acknowledge the unique challenges faced by these regions, such as remoteness, insularity, and economic dependency.

The new vision aims to ensure these regions can fully realize their potential, contribute to greater resilience, and offer better opportunities for their inhabitants. It also welcomes the Commission's commitment to a new horizontal approach for scrutinizing and potentially amending relevant legislation.

articles.headline: Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors
body: In this interim final rule (IFR), the Department of Commerce is establishing new rules to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on U.S. technology to threaten U.S. national security and foreign policy interests. First, this rule establishes new restrictions which will apply for exports, reexports, or transfers (in-country) to overseas data centers that remotely supply significant volumes of compute to companies headquartered in Country Group D:5 or Macau. These restrictions will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using U.S. advanced Super Intelligence (SI) semiconductors to train advanced SI models. Data centers, foreign foundries, and chip exporters are required to perform robust due diligence on their customers, including any direct or indirect ownership or control by persons in Country Group D:5 or Macau, as part of complying with this new control. The license requirement will not apply to commercial recommender systems, such as those used by online retailers or social media companies, as these functions do not pose the same national security threat. Second, in addition to the current license requirements for advanced semiconductors, a license will be required to export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil (and any additional country designated by the Secretary of Commerce, in consultation with the Secretary of State or the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs)--countries which present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion. The license requirement for these five countries will not apply to semiconductors destined to companies headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent company is headquartered in, the United States, provided certain reporting requirements are met. Commerce will be actively monitoring for countries that tolerate evasion of this IFR and will consider a range of consequences for such countries, such as import restrictions, new license requirements on advanced semiconductor exports, downgrading the country's status in the U.S. export control regime, and Entity List designations and temporary export prohibitions for foreign persons involved in such activities. Third, this IFR amends the presumptions which front-end chips fabricators and chip packagers face when exporting advanced-node logic chips. These amendments reduce the number of pathways to overcome the presumptions for chip designers located in destinations which face a license requirement for SI chips. This change gives the U.S. government critical oversight over companies headquartered in certain countries that seek to leverage advanced semiconductor production capabilities in third countries. Finally, the IFR formally rescinds the regulations implementing the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule. The AI Diffusion Rule has never been enforced. The regulatory changes in this rule formalize the rescission of the AI Diffusion Rule, which the Department of Commerce Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced in May 2025.

articles.headline: Revisions to the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) revises the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing two addresses associated with Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. from the Entity List under the destination of China, People's Republic of (China). This determination follows the removal from the Entity List of Arrow China Electronics Trading Co., Ltd., and the removal of six aliases for Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. in November 2025.

articles.headline: Removal From the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing one entity from the Entity List under the destination of Turkey.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.
